provenance: Opus 5.5 subscription CLI draft with host review/repairs, source restrictions and execution verification.

draft_notes.explanation:
In the original task the background is the most common colour. Every other colour forms one line. The lines are sorted by topmost row (minimum y), with minimum x as the tie-break. Their colours are then written as full-width bands into a 5x3 canvas. The bands are bottom-aligned, so the top is padded with background.

The factory tracks symbolically how the D4 transform maps original axes onto visible axes. The flip is applied first, then the clockwise rotations, using (r,c)->(c,H-1-r) for each rotation. From this it specialises three things in the emitted program, all in visible coordinates:
(1) Primary sort key. 'Original min y' becomes min or -max of the visible rows or visible columns, whichever carries the original row axis. A reversed axis turns min into -max.
(2) Secondary tie-break key. The same treatment is applied to the original x axis.
(3) Output geometry. The canvas is 5x3 or 3x5. Bands are rows or columns. They are filled bottom/right-aligned or top/left-aligned, depending on whether the band axis is reversed.

Colours are never remapped. The background is inferred as the most common colour, and band colours are copied straight from the line pixels. So the palette needs no special handling, and the demonstrations are not needed.
draft_notes.limitations: This assumes the generator's domain: one connected line per non-background colour, at most 5 lines, and a background that is strictly the most common colour. If there were more than 5 lines, the extra early bands would be clipped, as in the archived solver. Ties on both the primary and secondary keys fall back to ordering by colour value. Those ties cannot arise in this generator. The fixtures were consistent with the uniform rule, and no contradictions were found. I have not run any tests.
